clue.text: A place for experiments in money bears fruit

indicators.note: 'in money' puts the preceding phrase inside the word for money

parts.note: cash is ready money
a lab, short for laboratory, is where experiments are done

explanation.surface: A research laboratory's funding pays off handsomely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears fruit' reads as a verb phrase meaning succeeds; 'bears' is only a link and 'fruit' is the definition. 'In' splits the money word as C...ASH around the laboratory.
explanation.definitionFit: A calabash is a gourd, the hard-shelled fruit of a tropical tree or vine.

clue.text: Is the top general able to knock it back ?

definitions.text: Is the top general able to knock it back ?

indicators.note: 'knock it back' tells us each of the two pieces is turned round in place

parts.note: GOC stands for General Officer Commanding, the senior army general in a command
can means able to

explanation.surface: Asking whether the commanding general can down his brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns GOC into COG and CAN into NAC; 'knock it back' also means drink it, which is what one does with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognac is a French brandy, the sort of spirit a general might knock back.

clue.text: Get away from the point, causing ferment

parts.note: to leave a place is to get away from it
N, north, is one of the points of the compass

explanation.surface: Wandering off the subject stirs up unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The point' is a compass point, N for north, not the point of an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaven is yeast or another agent that makes dough ferment and rise.

clue.text: A copper-backed can overflowing with ale for the pirate

indicators.note: ale overflowing a can spills round it, so the word for ale goes around the other pieces

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

indicators.note: backed says the symbol for copper is turned round

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pirate's tankard: a can backed with copper and brimming over with ale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' turns CU (copper's chemical symbol) into UC; with CAN that goes inside BEER, signalled by 'overflowing with'.
explanation.definitionFit: A buccaneer was a pirate, especially one raiding Spanish colonies in the Caribbean.

clue.text: The chief sails unfashionably dressed

parts.note: a square is an old-fashioned person, so square means unfashionable
rigged means fitted out or dressed, as a ship with its sails and ropes

explanation.surface: The boss goes sailing in old-fashioned clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The chief sails' looks like a boss going sailing; it is the definition, describing a ship whose principal sails are square ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A square-rigged ship has its main canvas on yards set across the mast, so square sails are its principal ones.

clue.text: Dance jacket

explanation.surface: Just two words naming a dance garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolero is a lively Spanish dance in triple time, and also a short open jacket ending above the waist.

clue.text: Previews of some' women's fashions ?

indicators.note: some of the next word means only part of its letters are taken

explanation.surface: A preview of what women will be wearing next season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes part of WOMEN'S, dropping only the first letter; 'fashions' completes the surface picture of a fashion preview.
explanation.definitionFit: Omens are signs that foreshadow what is to come, giving advance glimpses of the future.

clue.text: Widespread ill-feeling — it's the same in poetry

indicators.note: 'in poetry' places the Latin word inside the word for poetry

parts.note: an epic is a long narrative poem
idem is Latin for 'the same', used in footnotes

explanation.surface: Bitterness everywhere, and verse is no better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-feeling' reads as resentment, but here means feeling ill: sickness that is widespread. The Latin footnote word for 'the same' goes inside the long poem, signalled by 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: An epidemic is an outbreak of disease affecting many people in a community at once.

clue.text: Where prompt attention is requested

parts.note: the prompter, who feeds forgotten lines to actors, sits in the wings out of the audience's sight

explanation.surface: A place where quick service is demanded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prompt' reads as quick, but it is the theatre prompt: an actor who dries calls 'prompt' and the prompter in the wings supplies the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Offstage means out of the audience's view, in the wings where the prompter works.

clue.text: In hue like the greasy Limpopo River? Just so

definitions.text: In hue like the greasy Limpopo River? Just so

parts.words: In hue like the greasy Limpopo River? Just so
parts.note: Kipling's Just So Stories describe the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, so the colour sought is grey-green

explanation.surface: A question about the colour of Kipling's African river, with a nod to his stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just so' looks like an agreeing tag but names Kipling's Just So Stories, where the Limpopo is 'grey-green, greasy'; the answer is the botanist's word for that bluish grey-green.
explanation.definitionFit: Glaucous describes a dull greyish-green or bluish-green colour, like the bloom on a plum.

clue.text: Outstanding work of art

parts.note: read literally, a sculpture whose figures stand out from a flat background

explanation.surface: Praise for a masterpiece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' reads as excellent, but here it means literally standing out: carved figures projecting from a flat surface.
explanation.definitionFit: In sculpture, a relief is a carving whose forms project from a flat background.

clue.text: Ward's "female woman" was one of the greatest of these

definitions.text: Ward's "female woman" was one of the greatest of these

parts.words: Ward's "female woman" was one of the greatest of these
parts.note: the American humorist Artemus Ward wrote that the female woman is one of the greatest establishments of the land, spelling it phonetically

explanation.surface: A quotation from a humorist praising womankind.
explanation.walkthrough: Artemus Ward, the 19th-century American comic writer, wrote that 'the female woman is one of the greatest institooshuns of which this land can boste'.
explanation.definitionFit: Institutions are established customs or organisations, such as marriage or a long-standing practice.

clue.text: Have a care crossing this palm!

indicators.note: crossing here means the letters are crossed over and mixed, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning to be careful when passing a particular palm tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossing' looks like walking past the palm; it is the signal to rearrange the letters of A CARE.
explanation.definitionFit: The areca is a genus of tropical palm, the source of the betel nut.

clue.text: Finding fresh vitality somehow near the trail

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of the word before are put together in some other way

parts.note: a scent is the trail an animal leaves for hounds to follow

explanation.surface: A tracker regains energy on getting close to the quarry's track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges NEAR into RENA; 'the trail' is the scent a hunted animal leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Renascent means being reborn or reviving, so it describes something gaining new life and energy.

clue.text: Under-cover sport for Sherlock Holmes ?

parts.note: Holmes is pictured in his famous peaked cap, so his pastime is one pursued under that cover, which is named after a hunter of deer

explanation.surface: A suggestion that the great detective enjoys a spot of secret undercover work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under-cover' suggests secret detective work, but the cover is Holmes's deerstalker cap, named after the Highland sport of stalking deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Deerstalking is the sport of hunting deer by creeping up on them on foot, and gives its name to Holmes's hat.

clue.text: Bid a dead-pan bestir himself ?

parts.note: a dead-pan face is lifeless, so one tells its owner to show some life and get moving

explanation.surface: Telling an expressionless person to get a move on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead-pan' means expressionless; the command to wake up and hurry plays on the 'dead', urging him to seem alive.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Look alive!' is an order to hurry up and be alert.

clue.text: Destroys vessels by fire

explanation.surface: Something burns the ships.
explanation.definitionFit: To scuttle a ship is to sink it deliberately; coal scuttles are metal containers kept beside the fireplace.

clue.text: One's outfit — surely not " the altogether "!

definitions.text: One's outfit — surely not " the altogether "!

parts.words: One's outfit — surely not " the altogether "!
parts.note: the French-derived word for a matching set of clothes literally means all together, yet 'the altogether' is slang for being naked

explanation.surface: A protest that someone's clothing should not be nudity.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a coordinated outfit comes from French for 'together', but 'in the altogether' means naked, the opposite of an outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensemble is a matching set of clothes worn together; the word also means the whole taken together.

clue.text: "Birds of a feather ."

parts.note: the proverb continues 'flock together', and a flock gathered together is a word for a church's assembled worshippers

explanation.surface: The opening of the proverb about like-minded people.
explanation.walkthrough: The unfinished proverb 'Birds of a feather flock together' points to a flock, the usual image for a church's gathered faithful.
explanation.definitionFit: A congregation is an assembled gathering, especially of worshippers, whom a pastor calls his flock.

clue.text: The sort to pass round for the collection ?

definitions.text: The sort to pass round for the collection ?

parts.words: The sort to pass round for the collection ?
parts.note: a collection is often taken in an upturned hat, and a metal helmet would serve well

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of container to circulate when gathering donations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass round the hat' is to collect money; a hat made of metal suits the coins, and a soldier's steel helmet goes by this slang name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin hat is a soldier's steel helmet.

clue.text: Mrs. Battle's favourite suit

parts.note: Charles Lamb's essay 'Mrs Battle's Opinions on Whist' says the old lady's favourite card suit was the red one with the love symbol

explanation.surface: A question of which outfit a lady preferred.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Battle is the whist-playing old lady of Charles Lamb's essay; 'suit' means a suit of cards, not clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts is one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards.

clue.text: The way to handle a mate in distress in the river?

indicators.note: 'in the river' puts the scrambled letters inside the river's name

parts.note: the Trent is a major river of the English Midlands

indicators.note: a mate in distress is upset and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice on looking after a shipmate who is in trouble in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In distress' rearranges MATE into ATME, and the second 'in' puts that inside the Trent, an English Midlands river. The 'a' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Treatment is the manner in which someone or something is dealt with.

clue.text: Subject for the master ?

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts degree; that the letters also run across the words 'the master' is a coincidence

explanation.surface: A topic set for a schoolmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: MA, Master of Arts, is the master; the answer is the old Greek-derived word for a theme, as set for an essay.
explanation.definitionFit: A thema is a theme or topic for discussion or an exercise, the Greek and Latin form of theme.

clue.text: A pay-increase can occur

parts.note: a rise is the British word for an increase in wages

explanation.surface: A remark that a salary increase may happen.
explanation.walkthrough: RISE is the British term for a pay increase (Americans say raise).
explanation.definitionFit: To arise is to come into being or happen, as a problem may crop up.

clue.text: Ono kind of worm and where one may' be found when knocked up

parts.note: the lob or lobworm is a large earthworm used as bait
a worm lives in a garden bed, the soil of a flower bed

explanation.surface: A gardener's note on worms and where they live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked up' is the definition: in cricket or tennis, a ball knocked up high into the air has been lobbed.
explanation.definitionFit: To lob is to hit or throw a ball in a high arc, so a ball knocked up high has been lobbed.

clue.text: Thora and Pip further mislead a misguided husband

indicators.note: the two names are misled again, sent astray, so their letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Two friends deceive a husband who has already been led astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Further mislead' rearranges THORA and PIP together. In Genesis, Potiphar was misled by his wife's false charge against Joseph.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible Potiphar, the Egyptian officer, believed his wife's lie that Joseph had assaulted her and jailed him.

clue.text: A playful saying from the bishop's throne?

definitions.text: A playful saying from the bishop's throne?

parts.words: A playful saying from the bishop's throne?
parts.note: a bishop's throne is his see, and a saw is an old saying, so a saying from it is a ..., the up-and-down plank children play on

explanation.surface: A bishop cracking a joke from his cathedral seat.
explanation.walkthrough: A bishop's seat or diocese is his SEE, and an old saying is a SAW; put together they give the plaything, also the nursery rhyme 'See-saw, Margery Daw'.
explanation.definitionFit: A seesaw is a balanced plank on which two children ride up and down in play.

clue.text: It's tho Serpentine one will never set on fire!

definitions.text: It's tho Serpentine one will never set on fire

parts.words: It's tho Serpentine one will never set on fire
parts.note: serpentine is a mineral group whose fibrous form is the fireproof material, while the Serpentine is also the lake in Hyde Park

explanation.surface: A joke that nobody will ever set London's Serpentine lake alight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set the Thames on fire' means to achieve something remarkable; the Serpentine is a lake in London's Hyde Park, but also the mineral whose fibrous form, chrysotile, is the fireproof material sought.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral that resists burning; the commonest kind, chrysotile, belongs to the serpentine group.
